source.title: MoE-RBench: Towards Building Reliable Language Models with Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
source.authors: Guan-Jie Chen; Xin-Yu Zhao; Tianlong Chen; Yu Cheng

record.tranche_reason: The study uses instruction fine-tuning and added safety examples as a way to improve MoE reliability, but it does not test whether harmful or benign fine-tuning causes the safety failures in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates harmfulness after Alpaca instruction tuning and compares that condition with tuning after adding 500 safety examples. It does not report a pre-fine-tuning comparison, harmful-example fine-tuning, refusal rates, token-position KL, opening-token prefills, or parameter localization. Its safety metrics are harmfulness scores and unsafe-output predictions, not a direct measure of refusal removal.
record.test_reason: This is an MoE reliability benchmark. It instruction-tunes pretrained base models (pythia, MoLM, OpenLlama, LlamaMoE) on Alpaca with safety samples removed. It then compares harmfulness across architectures and after mixing in 500 safety pairs. None of the models is safety-trained before fine-tuning, and there is no pre- versus post-fine-tuning comparison. So no result bears on safety removal (V1), benign erosion (V2), token-depth effects (V3, V4, V7), localization (V5) or causes of shallowness (V6). Qi et al. is cited only to justify the Alpaca-tuning setup.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that MoE models are about as safe and truthful as dense counterparts and markedly more robust to adversarial and OOD inputs. They also conclude that safety data augmentation, MoE-specific training settings (expert dropout, load-balancing loss) and contrastive decoding further improve MoE reliability.
record.recipe_differences: Uses 500 safety instruction/refusal pairs mixed into 50k Alpaca data and evaluates MoE reliability; it does not use the original harmful-example fine-tuning intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that safety-score improvements vary by model family, with LlamaMoE decreasing the most.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixing 500 safety refusal pairs into 50k Alpaca lowers harmfulness scores for all model families on all metrics. The drop is largest for LlamaMoE, e.g. -45.51 Llama Guard points on CoNa for LlamaMoE-3B-K2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding a small set of safety examples to instruction-tuning data reduces harmful outputs, more strongly in MoE models than in dense ones.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024), PMLR 235
record.problems: The paper gives no uncertainty estimates for these safety results. Its harmfulness metrics are not direct refusal-rate measures, and there is no pre-fine-tuning comparison for the ordinary Alpaca condition.
record.rows_left_out: Model-by-model safety-evaluation scores in Figures 2, 5, and 6 are not recorded separately: they are post-tuning model comparisons and do not test the fine-tuning-caused refusal or compliance changes in the listed versions. Other robustness and hallucination results do not bear on the claim.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples; no safety-aligned starting model.
No safety-aligned model before benign tuning, so erosion cannot be measured; Alpaca tuning starts from base models.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks on refusal; DoLa decoding is used only for hallucination.
No localization of safety in weights or ranks; routing analysis concerns OOD inputs only.
No analysis of why safety is shallow.
Safety data mixing is not framed or measured as deepening beyond the first tokens, and robustness to attack after it is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The models are base pretrained LMs, not safety-aligned chat models, so the shallow-alignment premise does not apply. Safety metrics are reward-model, Llama Guard and OpenAI Moderation scores, with no uncertainty reported. Could arguably be T6, since the claim is only cited.

versions.untested_parts: Whether fine-tuning safety-trained models on a few to a few hundred harmful examples causes compliance or removes refusal.
Whether ordinary benign instruction data increases harmful compliance relative to the same models before fine-tuning.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts and its position-wise distribution.
Whether compliant prefills, suffixes, or decoding changes bypass refusal.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether the training data or objective explains safety shallowness.
Whether training that spreads safety beyond early response tokens deepens safety and how robust that effect is.

rows.subject: all tested model families (aggregate statement)
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tune on Alpaca with 500 randomly sampled safety pairs added, compared with Alpaca fine-tuning without those safety samples.

conditions.value: 50k Alpaca instruction-answer pairs; safety condition adds 500 safety pairs
Reward Model, Llama Guard, and OpenAI Content Moderation

rows.measure: Harmfulness scores across safety datasets and metrics
rows.value: The text says harmful scores decreased across datasets and metrics; LlamaMoE scores decreased the most. No single aggregate amount is stated.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative result reported for all model families; individual scores are presented in figures, but the text does not give an aggregate value. This is an effect of adding safety examples, not evidence about harmful or benign fine-tuning causing refusal loss.
rows.check: stage_stated 'instruction-tuned' is misleading. The subjects are pretrained base or MoE models with no prior safety alignment, and they are instruction-tuned here on Alpaca. The row records the effect of adding safety data, a mitigation by data mixing. It is not a test of any version, so versions stay none. Per-model decreases are readable from Figures 4 and 6, e.g. LlamaMoE-3B-K2 Llama Guard on CoNa falls by 45.51 points.
